There a condition of affairs is described which I would ask any hon. gentleman in the House candidly to say whether he would like to have brought into force again in Manitoba and the North-west Territories; and the measure proposed here this afternoon is a measure calculated to cause a return of that condition of affairs.
Another plea that is made in behalf of the lumbermen is that they want the control of the Canadian market. 1 have taken some pains to look up statistics in connection with this industry, and so far as I have been able to ascertain, the lumbermen of Canada pretty well control the lumber market of Canada at the present time without any duty. Our exports of lumber amount in round figures to $25,000,000 a year. We import a little over $2,500,000 a year. The figures prepared in any of the departments of the government at Ottawa do not show what the total production of the lumber mills of Canada is; but so far as 1 have been able to ascertain by figures and calculations, I would place tbe total annual production of lumber in Canada at about $70,000,000. Of that, as 1 have said, we export about $25,000,000 worth and we import a little over $2,500,000; so that it would appear that the consumption of lumber in Canada amounts to about $47,500,000 worth annually. If these figures are correct and I believe they are, then the fact remains that the lumbermen of Canada at this Time have control of 95 per cent of the Canadian market; in other words, that the total importation of lumber does not amount to Mr. SCOTT.
over 5 per cent of the total consumpt.on of lumber in tms country.
Another argument wnich appeals to me as being the most weighty oue urged here this afternoon, is that we should impose a duty on lumber as an international measure-a measure which might have some effect upon our neighbours to the south. I am free to say that if I believed there was any real ground to hope that the imposition of a duty on lumber by Canada would lead the United States to give us reciprocity iu that article, I might be willing to agree to the proposition ; but it seems to me, in looking over the fiscal history of Canada and the United States, that there can be found not tbe slightest ground of hope that this would be the result. It seems to me that the history of the last eighteen or twenty years is bound to prevent any one who carefully considers the subject from believing or hoping that we can by the imposition of a tariff, bring about reciprocity between Canada and the United States.
So far as regards the statements made of the large sale of imported lumber, I have just given the House in round figures the amount of sales, and it is about 5 per cent or the total consumption of lumber in Canada. But even if the amount were larger, that would not be a good argument in favour of the imposition of a duty. It would simply be proof that our lumbermen were charging a little more than they ought, because Canada is one of the chief lumber producing countries in tbe world, and our lumbermen should be able to sell at prices which would prevent competition by the imported article.
Let me refer very briefly to a remark made by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), which would lead us to believe that, in his opinion, the members from Manitoba and the North-west Territories have rather outstayed their welcome in this House. He said that the older part of Canada had sacrificed or at least appropriated a great deal for the benefit of Manitoba and the North-west Territories ; and I think it is a fair deduction to make from liis statement that he thought it was high time for the western members to cease making any requests or taking any stand in behalf of the west in this House. Well, in my opinion, and in that of the other members from the west, the boot is entirely on the other foot. True it is that in the last thirty years considerable sums have been voted by parliament to be expended in and for the benefit of Manitoba and the Territories, and true it is also that large subsidies have been voted for railway construction there. But when we come to analyse this expenditure, we find that if there is any room for complaint by any one that complaint should come from "our "western people. When the Canadian Pacific Railway contract was made, $25,000,000 and 25,000,000 acres of land were voted to

that company. Something over half the subsidy was in land, most of which was located in the Territories, so that the people of Manitoba and the Territories themselves contributed more than half of Canada's total contribution to the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. And with regard to the votes passed every year for the carrying on of government in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, it must not be forgotten that amounts are apportioned by the statutes to the other provinces for the carrying on of local government. And I am in the judgment of every hon. member who has studied the position, when I say that man for man the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories pay a greater sum into the common revenues of the Dominion and receive less back from those common revenues than do the people of any other of the provinces.

As I have been always an ardent supporter of the national policy, Mr. Speaker, it will not surprise the House that I should rise to announce myself in favour of the present motion. I could give several reasons for this support, one of which is that I am firmly convinced that this motion is in the interests of the people generally, and not specially in the interests of the lumbermen.
I am also very much encouraged by the announcement of the Finance Minister a few evenings ago that we are on the crest of the wave of prosperity in this country, and by the remarks of my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). I have always looked upon that hon. gentleman as one of the most shrewd, level-headed, practical business men in this country, and ever since I came to this House I have listened with interest to his speeches. And although I have not always agreed with him, I have never failed to recognize the ability with which he invariably presents his case. On this occasion, I am quite sure that the hon. gentleman has been voicing the sentiments of the lumbermen and the agriculturists of this country. Some hon. members from the North-west have stated that British Columbia alone is in favour of an import duty on American lumber. I have the honour of being a member of the Ontario Association of Lumbermen, and although not an extensive lumber operator, I have been engaged in lumbering many years. That association had its annual meeting, and unanimously came to the con-clusioirthat it was necessary for the Canadian lumbermen to have an import duty on American products.
The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) says that he is a free trader. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am a free trader. I am willing to trade freely with those who will trade freely with me, but upon no other conditions, and therefore, 1 say that the Americans, having imposed a duty
upon Canadian lumber, the interests of our lumbering industry, which is second only to the great agricultural interest, demand the imposition of a duty upon American lumber.
In order to understand fully this question, I will have to give you a brief review of the legislation of the respective governments, provincial and Dominion, respecting the lumbering interests. In Ontario, limits have been sold by public auction, American purchasers and purchasers of all nationalities being invited to attend these sales. At that time, there was no restriction as _ to manufacturing logs taken from these limits. Sir William Meredith, who was then leader of the opposition in the legislature, wanted the government to stipulate that when any limits were sold the logs should be manufactured in this country. The government, in its wisdom, did not think fit to adopt this proposition, but continued to sell these limits. The government alleged as a reason why they did not wish to impose the proposed restriction that they would not be able to obtain as large a price for the limits as they would without that restriction. I suppose that that was all right. But let us see how the Canadian producer is discriminated against. Suppose that I am a Canadian lumber manufacturer and attend the sale and purchase a limit. An American attends the same sale and purchases the adjoining limit ; I invest, say, $100,000 in the erection of a mill, and providing plant to convert the logs on that limit into lumber. The American sends in his men and teams and removes the timber from his limit during the winter, takes it down the stream and transports it across the lake to his mill in the United States, say at Bay City or Saginaw. The offal of that mill, all the slabs and sawdust are valuable there. But I erect a mill on the Georgian Bay. The money that the American spends in taking out and transporting and cutting that timber is all spent in the United States. I employ Canadian labour, and every dollar I spend in taking out logs and converting them into lumber is spent in Canada. Suppose that the American, when he gets his lumber manufactured, does not find a suitable market for certain grades. He is permitted to ship his lumber Into Canada, irrespective of quality, without payment of any duty. On the other hand, if I want to send my lumber into the United States I am met with a duty of $2 per thousand. That is not right, it is not fair or just to the Canadian manufacturer ; it means that he is discriminated against and a preference given to the American. After the subject had been agitated a great many years, the government refused to impose an export duty. But regulations were made by the Ontario authorities stipulating that in the case of all limits sold or to be sold, the logs should be manufactured into lumber in this country. That regulation is carried into effect,

and tile result is tliat the Americans who bought our Canadian limits and who were taking the logs out of the country and manufacturing them in the United States are to-day manufacturing them into logs in Canada. But the injustice to the Canadian manufacturer still remains. That $2 per thousand is there. It should be removed. I know that very important and influential deputations have waited on the right hon. leader of the government and his colleagues who have met for the purpose of hearing their grievances. I believe the matter was very forcibly and ably put before these hon. gentlemen ; and I hope that, notwithstanding the announcement of the Finance Minister a few days ago, that no tariff changes would be made during this session, he will reconsider the matter. He should come to the conclusion that the poor lumbermen of this country deserve well at the .hands of the government, and that, not only in their interest but 'in the interest of this country, he should impose a duty on common lumber coming into this country. One hon. gentleman said that the United States was the only market we had for Canadian hardwood lumber. I beg to say that we cannot supply the demand in our own country. The Canadian furniture manufacturers have to import considerable quantities of hardwood lumber such as oak. There is no reason why, if I ship five or ten million feet of lumber to the United States and pay $10,000 or $20,000 duty for the privilege of doing so, the American lumberman, when he ships the same quantity Into this country should pay no duty.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cargill) a question ? if the Americans place themselves on a par with the Chinamen, is Canada to do the same thing ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards), I think, said that the Canadian lumbermen were of too large a calibre to condescend to approach this government and ask for the imposition of a paltry duty on lumber. Now, I think there are as good. [ as wealthy and as large lumber operators | in the United States as there are in Canada, and they have not failed to condescend to apply to the authorities for an imposition of a duty on Canadian lumber going into the United States. The hon. gentleman also says that such a duty would be detrimental to the interests of the farmer, and that the farmer cannot be protected.
1 claim, and have always claimed, that the farmers of this country have had more consideration than any other class in the community. Their grievances; have always been redressed when the government has been appealed to. I represent a rural constituency and have succeeded in being elected. And I have always stated to my constituents, a large majority of whom are farmers, that the farmer was the first man Mr. CARGILL.
considered by any government. How do we protect the manufacturer ? By placing a duty on goods similar to those which he produces, in order to prevent those goods coming into the country in competition with his. How can we protect the farmer ? By putting a little duty on beef, on pork and everything that would come into this country w-ere no duly imposed to compete in this market with the products the farmer has to sell. As I said before, the consideration of the farmer has always been first with the legislatures and the governments of this country. Why ? All governments are elected by farmers in this country, for the farmers are the majority. Of course, politicians are always looking for votes, and the way to get votes is to try to give the people who have the votes as great consideration as possible.
Reference was made to Mr. Waldie. I think Mr. Waldie is pretty well known in this country. He has had the honour of occupying a seat in this House. He is a very extensive lumber operator, and is president of the Ontario Lumberman's Association. I know that he headed large deputations to Ottawa on two or three occasions for the purpose of asking the government to impose a duty on American lumber. I do think and sincerely believe that the Finance Minister will eventually come to the conclusion that it is his duty to grant the request of the lumbermen, both of Ontario and of British Columbia.
Now, the lumbermen have never had any protection. I remember well that when the national policy was first proposed in this country a good many years ago, the hon. member for North Norfolk was not in sympathy with it. I remember reading a very fine speech made by that hon. gentleman on that occasion, in which he contended that the national policy would ruin the lumber interest. For instance, he gave the increased cost of the saws, and rubber belting, and everything the lumberman was likely to use in his business ; the imposition of a duty would necessarily increase their cost and increase the price to the lumberman. Now7, some gentlemen have said that the lumbermen have become millionaries. Well,
I do not know many of them who have. I think probably if that statement had been confined to the limit holders it might have been within the mark. I do know several gentlemen in this country who have bought limits, and 1 presume they made money out of them. Limits are usually put up at auction, and the purchasers have got to pay a higher price than any one else. But, I think it usually happens that they only hold them for a short time, until they find some one else who wants them worse than they do, and they sell them at a profit of a few thousand dollars. But the lumbermen are unfortunately not in that happy position. We have got to go to the bush, cut our logs, hitch up our oxen, and draw the logs to the

mill; aiul there is a great deal of hard work to be done before we succeed in making much money.
One gentleman said that the British Columbia lumbermen had not much to complain of, because they had to pay 50 cents freight per hundred pounds on the transportation of their lumber from British Columbia to Manitoba and the North-west Territories. That would amount to about $15 per thousand feet. Well, I think that the British Columbia lumberman who has to pay $15 per thousand feet in order to get his lumber to market in the North-west or Manitoba will not And much of a market there. That is a very high rate of freight to pay.
One gentleman said that only a small fraction of the lumbermen in this country were asking for the imposition of a duty, and he said that there were many lumbermen and especially the small millowners throughout the country, who did not want the duty. I admit that. But it is to be remembered that the majority of the sawmill men have a home market, they can sell their lumber in the nearest town, because there is generally some live industry in the town that uses all the lumber they can manufacture. Consequently we do not expect them to join in with the larger lumbermen who are forced, compelled in fact, to ship>
their lumber either to the United States or to Great Britain. Of course a large market has been created in Great Britain for what is called deals, a great proportion of the stock of that article finds its way to Great Britain. But there are many other grades of lumber which do not find a market locally, and it is that kind of lumber which comes in competition with lumber imported from the United States.
A few years ago I remember lumber took a jump upwards, when times were very dull. I remember one year several million feet of two-inch plank were brought from Duluth into the city of Toronto for sidewalks. The local dealers in the city of Toronto found they could bring lumber from Duluth and sell it cheaper than they could purchase it of Canadian lumbermen. No doubt that displaced just so much lumber manufactured by Canadians. I think on the whole that the lumbermen have made out a good case and that they are entitled to the consideration of this government. We hope that the government will consider the matter and impose a duty on American lumber coming into this country.
Now, the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) denied that there was any benefit to Canadians from the imposition of an export duty on logs, or the stipulation that logs should be manufactured in this country. He also stated that logs on the Georgian Bay were just as valuable as they were after they were cut up, and the manufactured article was piled up in the yard. That appears to me a very singular thing. We have some lumbermen on the Georgian Bay
who cut immense quantities of logs and manufacture them iu their mills; and if they can dispose of the logs for the same amount of money that they can dispose of the lumber when manufactured, 1 should not think they would go to the expense of manufacturing. The hon. gentleman imputes motives to people who stand up and want to protect their own industries. Well,
I suppose most men are built that way; and he would be the greatest philanthropist X ever saw if he did not condescend to say such things on some occasions.
Now, I think I am about through with all the remarks which I have to make on this occasion, but, I thought it was my duty to express my views upon this question. In conclusion, I will say that I do hope that after the frequent interviews which the Prime Minister and his colleagues have had with these important deputations that waited upon them for the purpose of getting that duty put on, they will give heed to the representations which have been made to them. I can only feel, and I believe, that the government will do what I consider would be most beneficial to one of the most important industries in this country.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to say a word or two in connection with this motion. I shall not take up very much time of the House, because I do not propose to say very much. If the people of the country gave to the government of the day a mandate at the recent election, that mandate was that there should be lower duties instead of higher duties. I think, that, in many of the discussions that took place throughout the country in connection with the election, the question of lowering the duties instead of raising them, was, to use a common phrase, a burning question with the people, and I am glad that the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) has sounded a note of warning, not alone for the benefit of the government, but for the benefit of hon. members on this side of the House, who, I am sorry to say, are drifting into harmony with protection principles, as shown in their speeches on the budget.	.
Name, name.

It is not necessary to give the names ; you can draw any inference you like. Any one who has listened to the remarks this afternoon from hon. gentlemen who support this resolution, will be convinced by the coolness with which they have approached the proposition. They tell us that the matter is for the general welfare of the country, that it is for the general welfare of the people at large. The agriculturists, of all other classes, are the ones who are to derive the benefit therefrom. They try to convey the impression that there is no selfishness in connection with this proposition. It seems to me that a duty of this kind, if it is going to affect anybody at all,

is certainly for the benefit of the particular class in whose behalf the duty is being imposed. I am not surprised that the people of the North-west Territories should feel hostile to a proposition of this kind, because they are subject, perhaps, more than anybody else, to what would be the outcome of a tariff on lumber. The manufacturers in every part of the Dominion, the manufacturers in small towns, as well as in the large towns, would be affected by a duty of this kind. Manufacturers tell us, that the present competition is such that they have to reduce the cost of manufacturing to the lowest possible basis in order that they may compete, not alone with the manufactures produced in their own land, but with the manufactures that come in from elsewhere, and that, in order to do so, it is absolutely pecessary for them to procure their raw material at the lowest cost. I agree almost entirely with the statement of the hon. member for Russell that we should guard as far as possible against an increase of duties and against an increase in the cost of manufacturing. It seems to me that the farmer bears the burden of it all. When the statement is made that the farmer derives a very i great indirect benefit as the outcome of the protective system, the author of that state-1 ment is simply throwing dust in the eyes of the farmer. The farmers derive no actual benefit from any phase of protection. They are the burden-bearers, and if there is an increase of duty on lumber or anything else the farmer has to bear the burden thereof. Just let me say another word or two, and it is this : I think that Canada should not be influenced by the legislation of the United States upon this point, or upon any other point. I think that Canada ought to legislate for itself. We should legislate in the interest of the people of Canada because they are our first concern. It may be true, as it is said, that we are adjacent to another country with interests and resources very much like our own, but, I think the principle that should guide us in this House, is the principle of our own interests absolutely and entirely, regardless of the interests of the adjoining community. The policy that should be adopted is the policy of mak-iag the cost of manufacturing and the cost of living as low as we can consistent with the requirements of the revenue of the country. I think that the government are entitled to commendation instead of condemnation for their attitude in connection with the delegations that have come down here. We know perfectly well the pressure that is [DOT]brought to bear upon the government by delegations that come down here representing their interests and asking that something shall be done for them. We know very well how hard it is for governments to resist the demands of deputations of that kind. We have, in the legislation of the past, evidence of the government having listened to the arguments that had been ad-Mr. HOLMES.
vanced, of having legislated in this direction, and then, having, the next day, to legislate in a counter direction in order to appease some rival interest. I think the government should be commended for not listening to the representations that have been made so far as the woollen interests, the lumbering interests, and other interests, are concerned, that have brought pressure to bear upon them in order to induce them to increase duties. I agree with the right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in his admirable speech the other night, wherein he said that the policy of this government should be in the direction of freer trade, of freer trade relations, in the direction of reducing, as far as we possibly can, the cost of manufactured articles, and therefore, I think, that the government are entitled to credit from the fact of their not having listened to the representations that have been made and not having yielded to the pressure that has been brought to bear upon them. They would have met my views even more largely had they seen their way clear to make some reductions in the tariff. While hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are tendering advice to the hon. Minister of Finance, it would have been a gratification to myself, I will say frankly, if he had seen his way clear to make a reduction on some articles which enter into the general consumption. There may be inequalities in any tariff, there may be matters that call for readjustment, there may be incongruities and to my mind there always are, and I think a man who is a protectionist out and out is placed in a contradictory position. He is called upon continually to extract himself from a difficulty of one kind or another because of the very policy he is endeavouring to support and to put into the tariff. A policy of protection is a policy of contradiction, and therefore, the position that those who support it are placed in, is such that they have constantly to excuse themselves for the position that it has led them into. I want to record my hostility to the proposition to place a duty on lumber, because I do not believe it is in the interests of the people as a whole, but that it is in the interest purely and simply of the lumbermen.

Mr. Speaker, my intention is merely to call attention to the interest of the North-west Territories in the motion which is under discussion this afternoon, and I do so because I think that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) probably left a misconception in the minds of some hon. members in quoting the Trade and Navigation Returns. He referred to the very small amount of lumber that is imported 'into the North-west Territories. But, I think he has only told half the story, because Manitoba and the North-west Territories gen-

erally go together in such matters as this. The liou. member for East Grey was correct when he said that the total importation of lumber into the North-west Territories was 707,000 feet, of a value of $7,505, but, he omitted to say that we imported into Manitoba 21,540,000 feet, of a total value of $272,471. The total value of free lumber imported from the United States was $574,233. Therefore, Manitoba and the North-west Territories put together imported 48 per cent, or about one-half of the total free lumber imported into Canada. The hon. gentleman will find that the other province which imported largely was the province of Ontario, and Ontario imported
8.768.000	feet, at a value of $205,452. Taking that lumber all round, it was lumber of the better class ; whereas, the lumber imported into Manitoba and the North-west Territories is of the cheapest kind, averaging only $12.50 per thousand. It would appear that the lumber imported into eastern Canada is principally for manufacturing purposes, or for finishing and the like, while the lumber imported into the west is for the erection of farm buildings, and for use by the man who puts up his wood shed until such time as he can raise money enough to build a house in front of it. The total import of lumber last year into Canada amounted to 36,309,000 feet, and of this quantity, 22,247,000 was imported into the North-west Territories and Manitoba. You will see that Manitoba and the North-west Territories imports more than two-thirds of this lumber, so that if the duty were increased there would be a most outrageous tax put on the people of the North-west, the people who have taken up farms, the people who have small means, and many of whom find it very difficult to gain a foothold for themselves and families. I wish to call attention to another matter which is in exactly the opposite direction to this. I assert that there is altogether too high a duty on lumber at the present time, and that it is too much protected. I find that last year there was imported into Manitoba
3.377.000	feet of dutiable lumber, valued at $45,279, and the duty on that was $11,319. The point is just this : that the dutiable lumber is lumber that has been dressed on both sides, or lumber tongued and grooved, but if we are to have free lumber, then I say that the duty should only be charged on the increased value given to that manufactured lumber by the labour spent on it in tonguing and grooving. As it is now, lumber is dutiable because it has gone through some manufacturing process, and the duty is charged on the original value of the lumber as well as on the labour expended on it afterwards. That is a grave injustice to the people who want free lumber. I am altogether opposed to this motion, which proposes to put a duty on lumber, and I am quite sure that the
North-west Territories, as well as Manitoba -which the hon. gentleman from East Grey very discreetly omitted to mention-are absolutely opposed to any such motion being adopted by this parliament.

My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue informs me that he has in contemplation to bring in at once a government Bill amending the Weights and Measures Act, and I would be glad -if my hon. friend would adopt the same course with regard to his Bill that I have just suggested with regard to other Bills, namely, that the whole matter be discussed under the government Bill, leaving his Bill on the Order paper, so that if necessary he can move it at a later stage.
Can that be done if the government takes the only day which is left to private members, as I understand they intend shortly to do ?

That is a very proper suggestion, and I think that before the government takes that day, there should be an understanding with regard to these Bills, so that the position of hon. gentlemen in charge of them would not be prejudiced.

I understand that when the government announced that they proposed to introduce legislation of a character dealing with a matter which is the subject of a Bill standing in the name of a private member, it was understood that if the government should change its plan, it should in good faith see that the hon. member who allowed his measure to stand at the request of the government should have an opportunity afterwards to bring it forward.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I quite agree that if the hon. gentleman allows his measure to stand at our request, we should see that he has an opportunity of bringing it on later.
May I ask if the government Bill embodies the principle of this Bill ?
I have a Bill pertaining to weights and measures to which may be added the provisions of the Bill now on the Order paper in the name of the hon. member.
speakername: The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE (Hon. M. E. Bernier).

speechtext: If that be the case, why should we not go into committee on the Bill, and let it pass the committee stage ?
Another reason is that the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) is not here to-night, and I know that he wishes to take part in the discussion on this question.

I should like very much that the Minister of Agriculture should be here, as I know he is well acquainted with the subject of this Bill.

On the order :
For resuming adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Robinson (Elgin) :	* That
inasmuch as almost every mile of railway in Canada has been aided, to a greater or lesser extent, by the Dominion government, the local legislatures, and the numerous municipalities through which they run ; and large sums of money have been given, as well as charters, conferring upon these railways a valuable franchise.
That inasmuch as the railways of the country are continuously seeking legislation for the advancement of some particular interest, or for securing some specific object ; which legislation occupies the time of this House at a considerable cost to the country.
That inasmuch as such legislation, in order to be effective for the purposes intended, should be well considered, both by evidence and personal inspection of the location affected, by the members of this House, to the end that the best interests of all parties concerned may be safeguarded.
That, in order that these ends may be satisfactorily attained, the different railway companies, for many years past, have given free transportation to all the members of parliament ;
And inasmuch as such free transportation, coming, as it doe_s, from the railway corporations, no doubt with a view of affording every facility to the members for obtaining the fullest information as to the needs and requirements, both of the railway corporations and the country, and, notwithstanding such free transportation is uniform to all the members of this House, the object and intention is largely misunderstood by the people, and construed into corrupt intentions on the part of the railway corporations, thereby subjecting both the railway corporations and the members of this House to an unjust and unfair criticism, which they are not always in a position to defend.
Therefore, in the opinion of this House, the present system of free transportation is unwise and undesirable, and should be discontinued, and a system substituted which would be 57
free from the charges of corrupt intention or from adverse criticism.
That inasmuch as the railway corporations receive more than adequate compensation for that service as now rendered ; this House is of the opinion that an Act should be placed on the' Statute-book making it incumbent on all railway corporations receiving a franchise or government aid either in money or land, to furnish free transportation to all members of this House, upon the certificate of the Clerk of the House ; and that no mileage indemnity be hereafter paid by the government to the members while in attendance upon their parliamentary duties.'

I do not suppose I am entitled to speak again on this question. It was thoroughly discussed when before the House on a former occasion, and I would like to have a vote upon it so that we might see how many members there are in this House who hold the same opinion on this question as I do.

I think it would be more satisfactory to my hon. friend to have a vote when there is a larger House than at present. He certainly could not expect tonight to get a very clear exposition of the views of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: The members of the government evidently anticipated a vote on this question, judging by their absence.

And apparently the leader of the opposition also.
